title: Overview and justification
body:
This course assumes you can already reference accurately and consistently, and that you already understand why academic work does so. What it adds is judgement under pressure: the ethical choices that referencing and attribution raise once you are working independently, in shared work, or in a professional role where getting it wrong has consequences beyond a lost mark.

By the end you will be able to justify your own course of action when a weak result tempts you toward a stronger impression than the evidence supports, and act to correct an unsupported claim in shared work. You will also be able to respond to a fairness issue around an unacknowledged contribution, critique your own habits against a profession's ethical expectations, and recognise and act on a new ethical responsibility without being asked.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  • Justify a course of action when a weak or disappointing result raises an ethical choice between honest reporting and presenting a stronger impression.
  • Justify acting to correct an unsupported figure or claim in shared work, upholding honesty even where the error would otherwise go unnoticed.
  • Justify a response to a fairness issue in shared work, weighing the discomfort of speaking up against the responsibility that courage requires.
  • Raise an unacknowledged contribution with those involved, treating them with respect, and help secure a fairer outcome even where the conversation is uncomfortable.
  • Critique your own habits of honesty and attribution against the ethical expectations of a profession, identifying where those expectations will tighten.
  • Recognise and act on an ethical responsibility in a new professional role without being asked, and explain the habit to someone newer than yourself.

title: In real academic practice
body: These are not abstract ethical puzzles. They are the situations that come up in a dissertation, a group project, a placement or a first professional role, where a weak result, an unattributed contribution, or an unfamiliar source type lands on your desk with no one checking your working. The judgement this course builds sits alongside your critical and research practice, informing the same honesty that underpins every claim you make and every source you cite elsewhere.

title: Signpost
body: The course has six short lessons, each built around a situation you might actually face. First, a weak result and the choice between honest reporting and a stronger impression. Second, correcting an unsupported claim in shared work. Third, a fairness issue in shared work. Fourth, raising an unacknowledged contribution. Fifth, weighing your own habits against a profession's expectations. Sixth, acting on a new ethical responsibility without being asked. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
instruction: Work through the six lessons in order.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Before you start, rate how confident you feel about each statement. There are no right or wrong answers.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.

_items.text: I can justify my course of action when a weak result tempts me to present a stronger impression than the evidence supports.
I can justify acting to correct an unsupported figure or claim in shared work, even if the error would otherwise go unnoticed.
I can justify my response to a fairness issue in shared work, weighing discomfort against the responsibility to speak up.
I can raise an unacknowledged contribution with those involved, respectfully, even when the conversation is uncomfortable.
I can critique my own habits of honesty and attribution against the ethical expectations of a profession.
I can recognise and act on an ethical responsibility in a new role without being asked, and explain the habit to someone newer than me.

title: Orientation
body: Not every result comes out the way you hoped. A weak result, a null finding or a small effect size is not itself a problem: it is information. The problem arises in how you choose to report it, because a weak result creates a genuine temptation to describe it in terms stronger than the data support.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are expected to recognise that temptation as an ethical choice, not a writing problem to be solved with better phrasing. The question is not how to make a weak result sound better; it is whether you report it as accurately as you would report a strong one.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Recognise an ethical choice raised by a weak result.
  • Classify a response to a weak result as honest or embellished.
  • Justify a course of action that reports a weak result honestly.

title: Concept: definition
body: An honest report of a weak result describes the outcome, including its limits, in the same terms you would use for a strong one. It uses no qualifier implying more certainty than the data support, omits nothing that complicates the narrative, and reframes no null or small effect as closer to significant than it was. Embellishment does not require a false statement; it is often achieved through selective emphasis, a softened verb, or a comparison chosen to flatter the result.

title: Concept: in practice
body: The temptation is strongest where the stakes feel highest. A dissertation result that falls short of what a supervisor expected, a pilot study that found no effect before a larger study is funded, or a project outcome due for assessment against peers whose results look stronger: each can trigger it. In each case the honest and the embellished report can describe the identical finding; the difference lies entirely in the language chosen around it.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have now distinguished an honest report of a weak result from an embellished one. The habit to carry forward is treating every result the same way before you know how it will look. Decide how you would describe a strong result, and hold a weak one to that identical standard rather than reaching for softer language only when the data disappoint you.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Think of a time your own result, data or outcome was weaker than you hoped. How did you choose to describe it in writing? Looking back, would you call that description honest, embellished, or somewhere in between?

No right answers are expected here; the aim is to notice the pressure before it shapes your next report.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A weak result is not itself a problem; the ethical choice lies in how you report it. You can now recognise that choice when it arises, and classify a given response as honest or as embellished even when no statement in it is technically false. You can also justify reporting a weak result in the same terms you would use for a strong one, as a professional default rather than a special favour to the data.

_items.title: See pages 185 to 187 of Chapter 10, 'Defining academic integrity', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: You are checking a shared draft, a dataset summary or a group report, and you notice a figure that nobody can actually support. No one invented it to deceive; it has simply drifted into the document unchecked and now sits there as though it were fact. Correcting it means admitting, to yourself and possibly to others, that something already circulating is wrong.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are expected to treat an unsupported claim as worth correcting even when nobody else has noticed it and even when raising it costs you something, such as time, an awkward conversation, or the comfort of leaving well enough alone. The claim's size is not the point; its lack of support is.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Identify an unsupported figure in shared work.
  • Justify correcting an unsupported claim that others would not notice.
  • Act to correct an unsupported figure in shared work.

title: Concept: definition
body: A claim is unsupported when no source, calculation or piece of evidence in the work actually establishes it, whatever confidence it is stated with. This differs from a claim that is simply wrong: an unsupported claim might turn out to be true, but the document gives the reader no way to check that, which is itself the problem. Correcting it means tracing the figure back to where it should be justified and either justifying it properly or removing it.

title: Concept: in practice
body: Unsupported claims rarely begin as deliberate fabrications. A number copied from an early draft survives several revisions after its source was cut. A rounded estimate, offered once in conversation as a guess, is later quoted as though it were measured. A figure from one context is reused in another where it no longer applies. Each has the same effect: a reader now treats as established something that was never actually shown.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have now distinguished an unsupported claim from one that is simply wrong, and practised tracing a figure back to whatever is meant to justify it. The habit to carry forward is treating silence, not confrontation, as the greater risk: a figure nobody checks does not become true because it goes uncorrected.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Think of a time you noticed, or suspected, an unsupported figure in shared work that nobody else seemed to question. What made you decide to raise it, or to let it pass?

No right answers are expected here; the aim is to notice what actually tips that decision one way or the other.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: An unsupported claim is one no source or calculation in the work actually establishes, regardless of how confidently it is stated. You can now identify such a claim in shared work, even when it has sat unquestioned through several revisions. You can also justify correcting it when nobody else would notice, because a figure's apparent acceptance by others is not the same as its being supported.

title: Orientation
body: In a group project, one member's contribution is visibly weaker than the rest, or one member has quietly done more than their share, and the final mark will be shared equally regardless. You notice this before the submission goes in. Saying nothing is the easier choice; it is also the choice that lets an unfair outcome stand unchallenged.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are expected to treat a fairness issue in shared work as something to weigh, not something to avoid. The discomfort of raising it is real, but so is the unfairness of leaving it, and neither cancels the other out. The question is how you weigh them against each other, not whether discomfort alone settles the matter.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Identify a fairness issue in shared work.
  • Weigh the discomfort of speaking up against staying silent.
  • Justify a response to a fairness issue in shared work.

title: Concept: definition
body: A fairness issue in shared work arises when the recognition, workload or outcome attached to a piece of collaborative work no longer matches what each contributor actually did. This can run in either direction: someone receiving credit for work they did not do, or someone doing work that goes unrecognised. Weighing the issue means setting the discomfort of raising it against the cost of letting an unfair outcome stand, rather than treating either consideration as automatically decisive.

title: Concept: in practice
body: The discomfort is rarely about the fairness issue itself; it is about what raising it might do to the group's relationships, its remaining time together, or your own standing within it. That discomfort is a genuine cost and worth naming honestly, rather than dismissed as mere squeamishness. But it is one cost among others: the unfairness continuing unaddressed, and what it signals about whether raising concerns in this group is safe, are costs too.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have now practised weighing the discomfort of raising a fairness issue against the cost of leaving it unaddressed. The habit to carry forward is treating that weighing as a genuine judgement each time, rather than defaulting to silence because confrontation feels harder than it is.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Think of a time you noticed a fairness issue in group work, whether or not you raised it. What did you weigh at the time, and would you weigh it the same way now?

No right answers are expected here; the aim is to notice what actually shaped that decision.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A fairness issue in shared work arises when credit, workload or outcome no longer matches what each contributor did. You can now identify such an issue, and weigh the discomfort of speaking up against the cost of staying silent, treating both as genuine considerations rather than letting either settle the matter alone. You can also justify a response that takes the full weighing into account.

title: Orientation
body: You have decided a contribution deserves acknowledgement it has not received, whether your own or someone else's. Deciding that is only the first step. What follows, the actual conversation, is where the decision either produces a fairer outcome or quietly stalls because nobody wants to make it happen.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are expected to carry a fairness decision through to an actual conversation, treating everyone involved with respect even when the conversation itself is uncomfortable. Respect here does not mean softening the point until it disappears; it means raising it in a way the other people involved can actually hear.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Raise an unacknowledged contribution with those involved.
  • Treat those involved with respect during an uncomfortable conversation.
  • Help secure a fairer outcome after raising a concern.

title: Concept: definition
body: Raising an unacknowledged contribution means naming, directly and to the people who can act on it, a mismatch between what someone did and what they have been credited for. This is distinct from simply noticing the mismatch, which this lesson's predecessor already covered. Doing it respectfully means focusing on the contribution and the outcome, not on blaming whoever overlooked it, and remaining open to the possibility that the oversight was genuinely unintentional.

title: Concept: in practice
body: The conversation is harder than the decision to have it, because naming an oversight can feel like an accusation even when none is intended. A supervisor who forgot to credit a contributor, a group member who took sole authorship by habit rather than design, or a collaborator who assumed their larger role was obvious: none of these need to have acted in bad faith for the correction to matter. Treating them with respect means allowing for that, while still insisting that the outcome itself gets fixed.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have now practised the difference between deciding a contribution should be acknowledged and actually raising it in a way that secures a fairer outcome. The habit to carry forward is following through: a fairness decision that never becomes a conversation changes nothing for the person whose contribution went unrecognised.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Think of a time you raised, or wished you had raised, an unacknowledged contribution, yours or someone else's. How did you balance directness with respect for the people involved?

No right answers are expected here; the aim is to notice what made that balance easier or harder in practice.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: Raising an unacknowledged contribution means naming a credit mismatch directly to the people who can act on it. You can now do this while treating everyone involved with respect, focusing on the contribution and the outcome rather than on blame. You can also help carry the conversation through to an actual fairer outcome, rather than treating the decision to raise it as the end of the matter.

title: Orientation
body: You have built habits around attribution and honesty over several years of study: ways of citing, correcting and acknowledging that you no longer think about consciously. Those habits got you through assessed work. Whether they are good enough for a profession is a different question, because professions are judged by a community of practice whose expectations do not automatically match a student's.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are expected to examine your own habits critically against the standards of a profession you are heading towards, rather than assuming a habit that has worked so far will keep working once the setting changes. The question is not whether your habit is honest by student standards; it is whether it would survive contact with a professional code.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Critique a personal habit of attribution against professional expectations.
  • Identify where a profession's ethical expectations will tighten.
  • Apply a community-of-practice lens to a personal honesty habit.

title: Concept: definition
body: A community of practice is a group bound together by shared standards for what counts as competent, honest conduct in their field: a professional body's code of conduct, an editorial standard, a regulatory requirement. Applying a community-of-practice lens means asking not whether your habit feels honest to you, but whether it would meet the explicit expectations of the community you are entering. Those expectations are frequently stricter than a student's, because the consequences of getting it wrong fall on other people, not just on a mark.

title: Concept: in practice
body: A habit that is adequate for an essay can be inadequate for a profession for several reasons. The stakes of an error are higher, the audience checking your work is more expert, and accountability is formalised through codes of conduct rather than left to a marker's judgement. A habit of citing roughly where an idea came from might satisfy a tutor; a regulator or editor may require an exact, checkable trail.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have now practised examining a personal habit against a professional standard rather than against your own sense of whether it feels honest. The habit to carry forward is treating this as an ongoing check, not a one-off exercise: each new professional setting may tighten the expectation again.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Think of a habit of attribution or honesty you currently rely on in your academic work. How confident are you that it would meet the expectations of the profession you are heading towards?

No right answers are expected here; the aim is to notice where the gap, if any, actually lies.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: A community of practice sets explicit standards for honest conduct that can be stricter than a student's own sense of what counts as honest. You can now critique a personal habit of attribution against those standards, rather than against how the habit has worked so far. You can also identify specific points where a profession's expectations will tighten, and apply that lens to examine your own habits before the setting changes.

title: Orientation
body: In a new role, most of what you do is told to you: a task, a deadline, a process to follow. Some things are not. You notice a gap, a risk or an oversight that nobody has assigned you to fix, and no instruction tells you to act on it. What you do next says more about your professional judgement than anything you were actually asked to do.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage you are expected to recognise this kind of unprompted responsibility and act on it, rather than waiting for someone to notice and assign it to you. You are also expected to pass the resulting habit on, explaining it plainly to someone newer than yourself, since a habit that stays unexplained does not outlast the person who first noticed it.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Recognise an ethical responsibility in a new professional role.
  • Act on an ethical responsibility without being asked.
  • Explain a professional habit to someone newer than yourself.

title: Concept: definition
body: An unprompted responsibility is one nobody has explicitly assigned to you, but which falls to whoever notices it first. It typically surfaces as a small gap: a safeguard nobody has checked recently, a record nobody has corrected, a risk nobody has flagged, because the structure around the role assumed someone would notice without being told. Recognising it means treating the absence of an instruction as neutral, not as permission to leave it alone.

title: Concept: in practice
body: New roles make this harder, not easier, because you are still learning what is actually expected of you and may assume that anything not explicitly assigned is therefore not yours to act on. Experienced colleagues often rely on exactly this kind of initiative without ever formally requiring it, which means the expectation can be real even when it has never been written down anywhere you have seen.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have now practised recognising and acting on a responsibility nobody assigned to you, and explaining the resulting habit to someone else. The habit to carry forward is treating this as a continuing part of the role, not a one-off test: each new gap you notice is another chance to act before being asked, and another habit worth explaining once you have.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Think of a time you noticed something in a new role that nobody had explicitly asked you to deal with. What made you decide to act, or to wait?

No right answers are expected here; the aim is to notice what actually shaped that decision.

title: Summary
displayTitle: Summary
body: An unprompted responsibility is one that falls to whoever notices it first, regardless of whether anyone has formally assigned it. You can now recognise this kind of responsibility in a new role, and act on it without waiting to be asked. You can also explain the resulting habit to someone newer than yourself, so that recognising and acting on this kind of gap becomes something the role teaches forward, rather than something each person has to notice alone.

title: Assessment introduction
body:
This is the test for the whole course. It covers everything you've studied in the lessons, with a set of questions to work through.

To pass, you need to score at least 70%. You can retake the test if you don't pass first time.

title: Confidence check
instruction: Now that you have finished the course, rate each statement again. You will then see how your confidence has changed.
_preConfirmation: Thank you. You will see these statements again at the end of the course, so you can see how your confidence has changed.
