title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course, and of this pathway. Referencing is no longer a mechanical or even a judgement skill: it is an ethical practice you can be trusted with. You can justify your own course of action when a weak result tempts you toward a stronger impression, and act to correct an unsupported claim in shared work. You can also respond to a fairness issue around an unacknowledged contribution, critique your own habits against a profession's ethical expectations, and recognise and act on a new ethical responsibility without being asked. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved, and carry this judgement into whatever comes next in your own academic and professional practice.

title: In real academic practice
displayTitle: Into your own practice
body: From here, this is a habit you carry rather than a course you finish. Notice the moment a weak result tempts you toward a stronger impression, and choose honest reporting anyway. Notice an unsupported claim or an unacknowledged contribution in shared work, and act on it even when the conversation is uncomfortable. This same ethical attention underpins the arguments you build in your academic writing and the rigour you bring to researching and investigating. It also runs through the judgement you exercise whenever you read and evaluate critically: it is not a separate strand of your practice but the integrity running through all of them.

title: Course Sources
instruction: This course draws on the following source.

_items.title: See pages 185 to 187 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

body: Your results are weaker than expected. Reporting them honestly risks a less impressive outcome than quietly rounding the figures favourably. What justifies the honest choice?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What justifies reporting a weak result honestly?

_items.text: The report's value depends on it reflecting what was actually found, not how impressive it looks.
_items.feedback: Yes. A report is only useful if it reflects what was actually found, however it looks.

_items.text: Honesty is only required when someone is likely to check the figures.
_items.feedback: The obligation doesn't depend on the chance of being checked.

_items.text: Rounding the figures favourably is fine as long as the difference is small.
_items.feedback: A small difference still misrepresents what was actually found.

_items.text: A weaker result reflects badly on the student, so presentation should compensate.
_items.feedback: Compensating through presentation is exactly the choice the question asks you to justify against.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The report's value depends on reflecting what was actually found, whatever the result looks like.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Weigh what the report is for against how it might look to a reader.

body: You notice an unsupported figure in a piece of shared work that no one else has spotted. What justifies correcting it rather than leaving it?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What justifies correcting an unnoticed unsupported figure?

_items.text: Honesty in the work doesn't depend on whether an error would be noticed.
_items.feedback: Yes. The standard to meet is honesty in the work, not whether an error would be caught.

_items.text: It only needs correcting once someone else raises it as a problem.
_items.feedback: Waiting for someone else to raise it leaves the error standing in the meantime.

_items.text: Leaving it is acceptable since the rest of the work is otherwise strong.
_items.feedback: The strength of the rest of the work doesn't excuse an unsupported figure.

_items.text: Correcting it is only necessary if your own name is directly attached to that figure.
_items.feedback: Shared work carries a shared responsibility for its claims, not just the one attached to a figure.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Honesty in shared work doesn't depend on whether an unsupported figure would otherwise go unnoticed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what honesty in the work requires, regardless of who might notice.

body: Raising a fairness issue in shared work means an uncomfortable conversation with people you work closely with. What justifies speaking up anyway?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What justifies raising an uncomfortable fairness issue?

_items.text: The responsibility to address unfairness holds even when raising it is uncomfortable.
_items.feedback: Yes. The responsibility holds regardless of how comfortable raising it feels.

_items.text: Speaking up is only justified once the unfairness has caused visible harm.
_items.feedback: Waiting for visible harm means the unfairness continues in the meantime.

_items.text: Discomfort is a sign the issue probably isn't serious enough to raise.
_items.feedback: Discomfort reflects the conversation's difficulty, not the seriousness of the issue itself.

_items.text: It is someone else's responsibility to notice and raise it first.
_items.feedback: Responsibility for noticing an issue doesn't transfer to whoever speaks first.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The responsibility to address unfairness holds, even when the conversation is genuinely uncomfortable.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Weigh the discomfort against what the responsibility actually requires of you.

body: A contribution to shared work has gone unacknowledged. What does raising it with those involved, respectfully, aim to achieve?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does raising an unacknowledged contribution respectfully aim to achieve?

_items.text: A fairer outcome, reached without treating anyone involved with disrespect.
_items.feedback: Yes. The aim is a fairer outcome, reached in a way that respects everyone involved.

_items.text: An admission of fault, regardless of how the conversation is handled.
_items.feedback: Securing an admission isn't the goal; a fairer outcome, reached respectfully, is.

_items.text: A record that can be used if the issue needs escalating later.
_items.feedback: Building a record for later escalation isn't the stated aim of raising it now.

_items.text: A quick resolution, even if it leaves the underlying unfairness unaddressed.
_items.feedback: Speed at the expense of fairness misses the point of raising it at all.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The aim is a fairer outcome, reached without treating anyone involved with disrespect.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a fair and respectful outcome would actually look like here.

body: You compare your own habits of honesty and attribution against a profession's ethical expectations. What should that critique help you identify?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should critiquing your habits against a profession's expectations identify?

_items.text: Where those expectations will tighten beyond what is currently required of you.
_items.feedback: Yes. The critique should surface where the profession's expectations go further than your current habits.

_items.text: Whether your current habits already meet every expectation you might ever face.
_items.feedback: Confirming that everything already meets expectations misses where the gaps actually are.

_items.text: That professional expectations and academic ones are essentially the same.
_items.feedback: Treating them as the same overlooks exactly where they are likely to differ.

_items.text: That habits formed as a student need no further attention once qualified.
_items.feedback: Assuming no further attention is needed is the opposite of what a critique should surface.

_feedback.correct: That's right. The critique should identify where a profession's expectations will tighten beyond your current habits.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about where the gap between your habits and the profession's standards is likely to appear.

body: In a new professional role, you notice an ethical responsibility that no one has asked you to take on. What does acting on it, and explaining it to someone newer, demonstrate?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does acting on and passing on an unprompted responsibility demonstrate?

_items.text: Recognising and acting on the responsibility without being prompted, and passing on the habit.
_items.feedback: Yes. Taking it on unprompted and passing the habit on both demonstrate the same ethical habit.

_items.text: Waiting until someone senior confirms the responsibility is yours to take on.
_items.feedback: Waiting for confirmation is the opposite of acting without being asked.

_items.text: Treating the responsibility as optional until it appears in a formal role description.
_items.feedback: An ethical responsibility doesn't wait for a job description to make it count.

_items.text: Assuming someone newer will work it out for themselves in time.
_items.feedback: Leaving it to be worked out alone is the opposite of explaining the habit to them.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Acting unprompted and explaining the habit to someone newer both show the responsibility has become genuinely yours.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what taking the responsibility on, and passing it on, actually requires of you.

title: Honest or embellished?
displayTitle: Honest or embellished?
body: A pilot study found no significant difference between two teaching methods. For each way of describing this result, decide whether it is honest or embellished.
instruction: Match each description to the correct category.

_items.text: "The two methods produced no significant difference in outcomes."
"The results suggest a promising trend favouring the new method."
"The difference approached significance."
"This small pilot was not powered to detect a difference of this size, if one exists."

_feedback.correct: Notice that embellishment here never states a falsehood; it borrows the language of a positive finding for a result that was not one. That is exactly the choice this lesson asks you to recognise.

_incorrect.notFinal: Check whether the phrase would lead a reader to expect a stronger finding than the data actually show, even if no individual word in it is false.

title: From most honest to most embellished
displayTitle: From most honest to most embellished
body: A study found a small effect size that did not reach statistical significance. Order these five descriptions of that single result from most honest to most embellished.
instruction: Drag the descriptions into order, most honest first.

_items.text: "The effect did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.09)."
"A small effect was observed, though it did not reach conventional significance thresholds."
"The effect approached significance, indicating a likely true difference."
"Results support the hypothesis, with a positive effect observed across conditions."
"The hypothesis was confirmed by the data."

_feedback.correct: The honest end of this order states the exact statistic and lets it stand; the embellished end claims confirmation the data do not support. The middle positions are where most real embellishment happens, through softened language rather than outright claims.

_incorrect.notFinal: Weigh each description by what a reader would reasonably conclude from it, not by whether it contains a false statement. The most embellished option need not lie; it only needs to overstate.

title: Worked example: reporting a disappointing dissertation result
displayTitle: Worked example

_items.title: Weaker approach
_items.body: {{learner-a}}'s dissertation finds no significant relationship between the two variables under study. In the write-up, {{learner-a}} describes the result as "a trend in the expected direction that approached significance" and devotes most of the discussion to studies that found a positive effect, mentioning the null finding only briefly near the end.

_items.title: Stronger approach
_items.body: {{learner-b}} faces the identical null result. {{learner-b}} reports it plainly as no significant relationship, states the exact statistic, and discusses it with the same weight given to a positive result: considering what the null finding might mean for the underlying theory, and what a differently designed study might still find. The discussion is shorter than a positive result might have produced, but it represents the actual evidence rather than a more flattering version of it.

title: Four subtly embellished phrasings
displayTitle: Four subtly embellished phrasings
body: Each phrase below could appear in a results section without an editor querying it. Weigh each one before flipping the card to see why it embellishes a weak result.
instruction: Select a card to reveal the reasoning.

_items.title: "Trending towards significance"
_items.back: Statistically, a result either reached the chosen threshold or did not; no intermediate state exists. This phrase borrows the language of significance for a result that lacks it.

_items.title: "Broadly consistent with the hypothesis"
_items.back: "Broadly consistent" can describe almost any result that is not a clear contradiction, including a null one. It implies support that the data may not actually provide.

_items.title: "A promising direction for future research"
_items.back: This is often true and often honest, but it can also be used to reframe a disappointing result as an opportunity, quietly skipping over what the current data actually showed.

_items.title: "Results were in line with expectations"
_items.back: If the result was weaker than expected, this phrase misrepresents the comparison between what was predicted and what was found.

title: Why honest reporting of weak results matters
displayTitle: Why honest reporting of weak results matters
body: Expand each heading to see a consequence of embellishing a weak result.
instruction: Select a heading to expand it.

_items.title: For anyone who builds on your work
_items.body: A researcher who later tries to replicate or extend an embellished finding is working from a false premise about how strong the original evidence was.

_items.title: For the field's evidence base
_items.body: Null and weak results that are reframed as positive distort the published record on a question, making the overall evidence look stronger than it is.

_items.title: For your own credibility
_items.body: A pattern of embellishment, once noticed by a supervisor or reviewer, affects how your future results are read, including the honest ones.

_items.title: For the decision the result informs
_items.body: If a weak result feeds into a real decision, such as whether to fund a larger study, an embellished description can lead to a decision the actual evidence does not support.

title: Heuristics for reporting a weak result honestly
displayTitle: Heuristics for reporting a weak result honestly
body:
These are checks to weigh against your own report, not steps to follow in sequence.

  • Have you stated the exact statistic or outcome, rather than a qualitative phrase that could be read as stronger?
  • Would you have used this same language if the result had come out the way you hoped?
  • Have you avoided phrases that borrow the vocabulary of significance for a result that did not reach it?
  • Have you given the weak result the same discussion space you would give a strong one, rather than mentioning it briefly and moving on?
  • Have you disclosed any exclusions, subsets or reanalyses that make the result look better than the full data would?

title: Check 1
instruction: A student's experiment produces a much smaller effect than expected. Which best describes the ethical choice this raises?

_items.text: Whether to rerun the experiment until a larger effect appears.
Whether to describe the result in the same terms as a stronger result would warrant.
Whether the experiment was designed correctly.
Whether to include the result in the final report at all.

_feedback.correct: The ethical choice is not about the result itself, which cannot be changed, but about the language used to describe it: whether that language matches the data or borrows the vocabulary of a stronger finding.

_incorrect.notFinal: The result itself is already fixed by this point. Think about what decision remains open once the data are in.

title: Check 2
instruction: A results section describes a non-significant finding as "approaching significance and consistent with a true effect". What makes this description embellished rather than honest?

_items.text: It contains a factually false statistic.
It claims a degree of support for the hypothesis that the data did not reach.
It is too technical for a general reader to understand.
It omits the sample size used in the study.

_feedback.correct: Embellishment of this kind rarely depends on a false statistic. It depends on language that implies a stronger finding than the result actually supports, which is exactly what happened here.

_incorrect.notFinal: Look for whether any individual fact stated is false, or whether the overall impression the phrase creates goes beyond what the data show.

title: Check 3
instruction: You have a weak result to report in a piece of work for {{context}}. What is the strongest justification for reporting it honestly rather than in stronger terms?

_items.text: An honest report is easier to write than an embellished one.
An honest report holds the result to the same standard you would apply if it had turned out well, and keeps the evidence base reliable for anyone who builds on it.
Markers rarely read the results section closely enough to notice embellishment.
A weak result reported honestly will usually receive a higher mark than one reported in stronger terms.

_feedback.correct: The justification is not about ease, detection risk, or marks. It is that honest reporting applies one consistent standard regardless of outcome, and that anyone relying on your result later is relying on an accurate account of it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about why honest reporting matters even when nobody would notice the embellishment. The justification should hold regardless of who is checking.

title: Supported or unsupported?
displayTitle: Supported or unsupported?
body: A group report contains several figures. For each one, decide whether it is supported by something in the document or unsupported.
instruction: Match each figure to the correct category.

_items.text: "62% of respondents agreed (n = 48, see Table 2)."
"Most students find this approach more effective." (no citation or data given anywhere in the report)
"Costs fell by around a third." (figure appears only here, with no source, calculation or earlier mention)
"Response time improved from 4.2 to 2.1 seconds (see Section 3.1 for method)."

_feedback.correct: Notice that an unsupported figure can sound just as precise and confident as a supported one. The difference is never in the tone of the sentence; it is in whether the document gives a reader any way to check it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Look for whether a reader could trace the figure to a source, a table, a calculation or a method described somewhere in the document, not for whether the figure sounds plausible.

title: From most to least likely to need correcting first
displayTitle: From most to least likely to need correcting first
body: A shared draft contains four figures, each raising a different kind of doubt. Order them from the one you would investigate first to the one you would investigate last, based on how much the final document relies on it.
instruction: Drag the figures into order, most urgent first.

_items.text: A headline statistic quoted in the executive summary and repeated three more times in the report.
A supporting figure used once, in a single paragraph, to illustrate a minor point.
A number used only in an appendix table that the main text never refers back to.
A rounded estimate explicitly flagged in the text as "approximate, pending confirmation".

_feedback.correct: Urgency here tracks how much weight the document places on the figure and how clearly its uncertainty is already disclosed, not how large the number itself is. A flagged estimate is already honest about its status; a repeated headline figure is not.

_incorrect.notFinal: Weigh how much a reader's overall impression of the document depends on each figure, and whether its uncertain status is already visible to that reader.

title: Worked example: a figure that drifted into a shared report
displayTitle: Worked example

_items.title: Weaker approach
_items.body: Reviewing the group report before submission, {{learner-a}} notices that the claim "adoption increased by 40% over the period" cannot be traced to any table, source or calculation in the document. Rather than raise it with the group so close to the deadline, {{learner-a}} leaves it as it is, reasoning that the marker is unlikely to check every figure.

_items.title: Stronger approach
_items.body: {{learner-b}} notices the same unsupported claim. {{learner-b}} messages the group to ask where the 40% figure came from, and when nobody can point to a source, proposes either finding the original calculation or rewording the claim to state only what the data actually show. The group agrees to the second option, and the final report describes the change in terms it can actually support.

title: Four ways an unsupported claim survives unnoticed
displayTitle: Four ways an unsupported claim survives unnoticed
body: Each situation below describes how an unsupported figure can persist in shared work. Weigh each one before flipping the card to see the risk it carries.
instruction: Select a card to reveal the reasoning.

_items.title: It appears early and gets copied forward
_items.back: Once a figure is in a draft, later editors often treat its presence as evidence that it was already checked, rather than checking it themselves.

_items.title: It sounds precise
_items.back: A specific number, such as 40% rather than "a lot", reads as more credible, even though precision says nothing about whether the figure is actually supported.

_items.title: Everyone assumes someone else checked it
_items.back: In group work, responsibility for verifying a shared figure can diffuse across the group until no one individual has actually traced it.

_items.title: Correcting it feels disproportionate
_items.back: A small, easily fixed error can go unaddressed simply because raising it feels like more trouble than the figure's apparent importance warrants.

title: Why correcting an unsupported claim matters, even a small one
displayTitle: Why correcting an unsupported claim matters, even a small one
body: Expand each heading to see a consequence of leaving an unsupported claim uncorrected.
instruction: Select a heading to expand it.

_items.title: For the group's shared responsibility
_items.body: Everyone whose name is on the work is implicitly vouching for figures they did not personally verify, including this one.

_items.title: For anyone who cites the work later
_items.body: A reader who quotes the unsupported figure in their own work inherits a claim that was never actually established, and passes that on again.

_items.title: For the habit it builds
_items.body: Letting one unsupported claim pass because it seemed too small to matter makes it easier to let the next one pass too, including a larger one.

_items.title: For the document's overall credibility
_items.body: A single traceable error, once found by a reader or marker, can prompt them to question every other figure in the work, not just the one that was wrong.

title: Heuristics for weighing whether to raise an unsupported claim
displayTitle: Heuristics for weighing whether to raise an unsupported claim
body:
These are checks to weigh against a figure you are unsure about, not steps to follow in sequence.

  • Could you point to the exact source, table or calculation that justifies this figure, if asked?
  • Has this figure been repeated or built on elsewhere in the document, increasing how much rides on it?
  • Would raising it now cost less than leaving it to be found later, by a marker, a reader or someone who cites the work?
  • Is there a quick way to confirm or correct it, such as asking whoever first added it, rather than assuming the worst?
  • Would you want someone else to raise an equivalent figure of yours, if the situation were reversed?

title: Check 1
instruction: A shared report states a figure that no table, source or calculation in the document actually establishes. Which best describes why this is a problem, even if the figure later turns out to be roughly correct?

_items.text: Because any figure that cannot be traced is necessarily false.
Because a reader has no way to check it, regardless of whether it happens to be accurate.
Because unsupported figures are always larger than supported ones.
Because the group will lose marks for including any unverified number.

_feedback.correct: An unsupported claim's problem is not its accuracy, which may be fine, but its traceability. A reader cannot tell the difference between a correct guess and a careful calculation unless the document shows its working.

_incorrect.notFinal: Separate the question of whether the figure is true from the question of whether the document gives a reader any way to verify it.

title: Check 2
instruction: You notice an unsupported figure in a group report two days before submission. Raising it will mean reopening a section the group considers finished. What is the strongest justification for raising it anyway?

_items.text: The group is less likely to notice a late change than an early one.
The timing of the deadline does not change whether the figure is actually supported, and the document will carry the error regardless of when it is raised.
Markers always check figures against their original sources.
Reopening a finished section is never disruptive if the correction is small.

_feedback.correct: Deadline pressure changes how inconvenient a correction feels; it does not change whether the underlying figure is supported. The justification for raising it holds regardless of timing.

_incorrect.notFinal: Consider what would still be true about the figure even if the deadline were further away.

title: Check 3
instruction: You have found an unsupported figure in a piece of shared work for {{context}}, and nobody else in the group seems to have noticed. What should you do?

_items.text: Leave it, since you are not responsible for figures you did not personally add.
Raise it with whoever can trace or correct it, since your name is also attached to the final document.
Remove it yourself without telling anyone, to avoid an awkward conversation.
Wait to see whether the marker notices it first.

_feedback.correct: Shared authorship means the figure's accuracy is partly your responsibility too, whoever first added it. Raising it openly, rather than silently fixing or silently ignoring it, keeps the correction transparent to the rest of the group.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about who the final document actually belongs to, and what that implies about who should know a correction is being made.

title: Fairness issue or ordinary group friction?
displayTitle: Fairness issue or ordinary group friction?
body: Group projects involve many small frustrations. For each situation, decide whether it is a genuine fairness issue affecting credit or outcome, or ordinary group friction that does not.
instruction: Match each situation to the correct category.

_items.text: One member consistently misses meetings but will receive the same mark as everyone else.
Two members disagree about which font to use for the report.
One member rewrites a section after another member already finished it, without discussion, and takes sole credit in the author list.
The group spends an extra meeting deciding on a shared referencing style.

_feedback.correct: The distinguishing question is whether the situation changes what credit, workload or outcome each person actually receives. Friction over preferences or process does not; a mismatch between contribution and credit does.

_incorrect.notFinal: Ask whether the situation would still bother you after the project ended and the mark was in, or whether it is the kind of disagreement that resolves itself once the work is done.

title: From easiest to hardest to raise
displayTitle: From easiest to hardest to raise
body: Four fairness issues differ in how comfortable they would be to raise with the group. Order them from easiest to hardest, based on what raising each one would risk.
instruction: Drag the issues into order, easiest first.

_items.text: A new member joined late and has not yet been assigned a fair share of the remaining work.
A long-standing friend in the group has contributed noticeably less than everyone else.
The group's most assertive member has taken credit for a section someone quieter actually wrote.
Raising the issue would mean contradicting what the group has already told the module tutor.

_feedback.correct: Difficulty here tracks the relationships and stakes involved, not the size of the unfairness itself. A fairness issue that is easy to raise can still matter, and a hard one does not become less real for being uncomfortable.

_incorrect.notFinal: Weigh what raising each issue would put at risk: a friendship, a power imbalance in the group, or a statement already made to someone outside the group.

title: Worked example: noticing an uneven contribution before submission
displayTitle: Worked example

_items.title: Weaker approach
_items.body: Two days before submission, {{learner-a}} realises that one group member has contributed almost nothing, while the mark will be shared equally. {{learner-a}} decides against raising it, reasoning that the deadline is too close and the conversation would only create tension the group does not have time for.

_items.title: Stronger approach
_items.body: {{learner-b}} notices the same imbalance. {{learner-b}} weighs the discomfort of raising it against the cost of staying silent, and decides the unfairness is serious enough to outweigh the awkwardness, especially so close to the deadline. {{learner-b}} raises it calmly with the group, proposing that the contribution be acknowledged in the submission rather than left unaddressed, and the group agrees to add a brief statement of individual contributions.

title: Four reasons silence feels like the easier choice
displayTitle: Four reasons silence feels like the easier choice
body: Each reason below can make staying silent feel like the obvious choice when a fairness issue arises. Weigh each one before flipping the card to see why it does not settle the question on its own.
instruction: Select a card to reveal the reasoning.

_items.title: "It's not worth the conflict"
_items.back: This weighs the discomfort of conflict but says nothing about the cost of the unfairness continuing, which is the other side of the judgement.

_items.title: "They probably don't realise"
_items.back: This may be true, but it is itself a reason to raise the issue directly, not a reason to assume it will resolve on its own.

_items.title: "It will all balance out eventually"
_items.back: This assumes a future correction that the current piece of work has no mechanism to guarantee, especially once marks are submitted.

_items.title: "I don't want to seem difficult"
_items.back: Raising a genuine fairness issue calmly and directly is different from being difficult; conflating the two makes every fairness issue harder to raise.

title: What staying silent actually costs
displayTitle: What staying silent actually costs
body: Expand each heading to see a cost of leaving a fairness issue unaddressed.
instruction: Select a heading to expand it.

_items.title: For the person whose contribution is overlooked
_items.body: Their work goes unrecognised in the mark and the record, with no mechanism left to correct it once the submission is in.

_items.title: For the group's future collaboration
_items.body: An unaddressed imbalance can repeat in the next project, since nothing in this one signalled that it mattered.

_items.title: For your own standing in the group
_items.body: Staying silent on an issue you noticed, if it later becomes visible to others, can look like tacit agreement rather than neutrality.

_items.title: For what the group considers normal
_items.body: Each unaddressed fairness issue quietly resets what the group treats as acceptable, making the next one easier to overlook too.

title: Heuristics for weighing whether to raise a fairness issue
displayTitle: Heuristics for weighing whether to raise a fairness issue
body:
These are checks to weigh against a specific fairness issue, not steps to follow in sequence.

  • Does the issue affect what credit, workload or outcome someone actually receives, rather than just how the group works together?
  • Is there still time for raising it to change the outcome, or has that window already closed?
  • What would staying silent signal to the rest of the group about whether fairness issues get raised here?
  • Is there a way to raise it that focuses on the outcome rather than assigning blame?
  • Would you want someone to raise an equivalent issue on your behalf, if the situation were reversed?

title: Check 1
instruction: Two group members disagree about which referencing software to use, while a third member's substantial unrecognised contribution goes unmentioned in the final submission. Which is the fairness issue?

_items.text: The referencing software disagreement, because it was never resolved.
The unrecognised contribution, because it changes what credit someone actually receives.
Both, because any unresolved disagreement in a group is a fairness issue.
Neither, because the group reached a submission despite both issues.

_feedback.correct: A fairness issue specifically concerns a mismatch between contribution and the credit, workload or outcome attached to it. A process disagreement, however unresolved, does not by itself change what anyone actually receives.

_incorrect.notFinal: Ask which situation actually changes what someone receives in credit or outcome, rather than which one simply caused friction.

title: Check 2
instruction: You notice a fairness issue in shared work, but raising it would mean an uncomfortable conversation with a friend in the group. What is the strongest way to weigh this?

_items.text: Since the discomfort involves a friend, it automatically outweighs the fairness issue.
The discomfort of the conversation and the cost of the unfairness continuing are both genuine; neither automatically outweighs the other.
Friendships should never be put at risk over a group project mark.
Fairness issues involving friends are not worth raising, since they resolve themselves eventually.

_feedback.correct: Treating the friendship as automatically decisive, in either direction, skips the actual weighing. Both the discomfort and the unfairness are real costs, and the judgement lies in weighing them against each other in this specific case.

_incorrect.notFinal: Consider whether either consideration, the friendship or the fairness issue, should settle the matter on its own, or whether both need weighing together.

title: Check 3
instruction: You have identified a fairness issue in a piece of shared work for {{context}}, and weighed the discomfort of raising it against the cost of staying silent. What should your response be based on?

_items.text: Whichever response avoids any discomfort for you personally.
The outcome of your weighing, expressed in a way that focuses on the issue rather than assigning blame.
Waiting until after submission, so the response cannot affect the mark either way.
Raising it anonymously, so no one can connect the concern back to you.

_feedback.correct: A justified response follows from the weighing itself, and is framed around the fairness issue rather than around protecting yourself or assigning blame, which tends to make the conversation harder rather than more productive.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what your weighing was actually for, and what a response that reflects it, rather than one that avoids it, would look like.

title: Respectful or accusatory?
displayTitle: Respectful or accusatory?
body: Each opening line below starts a conversation about an unacknowledged contribution. For each one, decide whether it is respectful or accusatory.
instruction: Match each opening line to the correct category.

_items.text: "I think my section of the analysis might have been missed from the author list, can we check?"
"You deliberately left my name off this, didn't you?"
"It's obvious you only credited yourself because you always do this."
"I want to flag something about the contribution list before we submit, do you have a minute?"

_feedback.correct: Respectful openings name the outcome and invite a shared look at it. Accusatory ones assume intent and character before the other person has had a chance to respond, which tends to make the conversation harder rather than more productive.

_incorrect.notFinal: Check whether the line assumes a deliberate motive or a pattern of behaviour, or whether it simply names the outcome and opens a conversation about it.

title: From most to least likely to secure a fairer outcome
displayTitle: From most to least likely to secure a fairer outcome
body: Four ways of following up after raising an unacknowledged contribution differ in how likely they are to actually change the outcome. Order them from most to least likely to succeed.
instruction: Drag the follow-ups into order, most likely first.

_items.text: Agree a concrete change (such as an updated author list) and a date to confirm it has been made.
Raise it once, accept whatever response comes back, and move on regardless of what was agreed.
Mention it in passing during an unrelated conversation, without naming what you want to happen.
Raise it clearly, propose a specific fix, but never follow up to check it happened.

_feedback.correct: Securing a fairer outcome depends on the conversation producing a concrete, checkable change, not just on the concern being heard. A clear ask with a follow-up date is far more likely to change anything than a clear ask left to chance.

_incorrect.notFinal: Weigh how specific the proposed fix is and whether anything is in place to confirm it actually happens, not just whether the concern was raised.

title: Worked example: raising a missed acknowledgement
displayTitle: Worked example

_items.title: Weaker approach
_items.body: {{learner-a}} notices that a collaborator's substantial contribution to the data analysis was left out of the final report's acknowledgements. {{learner-a}} mentions it once, in a brief and vague way, during a group call, and when nobody responds directly, lets the matter drop rather than raising it again.

_items.title: Stronger approach
_items.body: {{learner-b}} notices the same omission. {{learner-b}} raises it directly and privately with whoever can update the report, naming the specific contribution and proposing a specific fix: adding the collaborator's name to the acknowledgements before submission. {{learner-b}} agrees a date to confirm the change has been made, and follows up on that date rather than assuming it happened.

title: Four moves that keep a conversation respectful under pressure
displayTitle: Four moves that keep a conversation respectful under pressure
body: An uncomfortable conversation can drift towards blame even when that is not the intention. Weigh each move below before flipping the card to see why it helps.
instruction: Select a card to reveal the reasoning.

_items.title: Naming the outcome, not the motive
_items.back: Describing what happened ("the contribution wasn't credited") rather than why ("you didn't want to share credit") leaves room for an explanation you haven't yet heard.

_items.title: Proposing a specific fix
_items.back: A concrete suggestion gives the other person something to agree to, rather than leaving them to guess what you actually want to happen.

_items.title: Choosing a private moment
_items.back: Raising a credit concern in front of others can make it harder for anyone to respond calmly, whatever the actual issue turns out to be.

_items.title: Staying open to being wrong about the cause
_items.back: An oversight is often genuinely accidental; assuming the worst explanation before asking makes the conversation defensive rather than productive.

title: Why following through matters, not just raising it
displayTitle: Why following through matters, not just raising it
body: Expand each heading to see why raising a concern is not the same as resolving it.
instruction: Select a heading to expand it.

_items.title: Agreement is not the same as action
_items.body: Someone can agree in the moment that a contribution should be credited and still forget, or deprioritise, actually making the change.

_items.title: The outcome is what the person whose contribution was missed actually cares about
_items.body: Being heard matters, but it does not change the record on its own; only the correction itself does that.

_items.title: Checking back keeps the correction visible
_items.body: A brief follow-up signals that the issue still matters, without needing to repeat the original conversation.

_items.title: Unresolved concerns tend to resurface, less calmly
_items.body: If the fix never happens, the same issue often returns later, at a worse time and with more frustration attached.

title: Heuristics for raising an unacknowledged contribution
displayTitle: Heuristics for raising an unacknowledged contribution
body:
These are checks to weigh when preparing for the conversation, not steps to follow in sequence.

  • Have you named the outcome you noticed, rather than the motive you suspect?
  • Do you have a specific fix in mind, rather than just a concern?
  • Is this a private moment, rather than one that puts anyone on the spot in front of others?
  • Have you left room for an explanation you haven't yet heard, rather than assuming the worst?
  • Have you agreed, or will you agree, a way to confirm the fix actually happens?

title: Check 1
instruction: You are preparing to raise an unacknowledged contribution with the person responsible for the final document. Which opening best raises it while treating them with respect?

_items.text: "I noticed my contribution to the data section wasn't included in the acknowledgements, can we take a look?"
"You clearly didn't think my work was worth mentioning."
"This is exactly the kind of thing you always do."
Saying nothing and hoping the next version corrects it automatically.

_feedback.correct: The respectful opening names the specific outcome and invites a shared look at it, without assuming a motive or a pattern of behaviour before the other person has had a chance to respond.

_incorrect.notFinal: Separate what actually happened (the outcome) from what you suspect about why it happened (the motive), and lead with the former.

title: Check 2
instruction: During a conversation about an unacknowledged contribution, the other person seems to have genuinely forgotten rather than acted deliberately. How should this change your approach, while treating them with respect?

_items.text: It means the issue no longer needs fixing, since there was no bad intent.
The fix still needs to happen; an unintentional oversight does not lessen the outcome for the person whose contribution was missed.
You should apologise for raising it, since it turned out to be accidental.
You should let it go this time, and only raise it if it happens again.

_feedback.correct: Respect for the other person's likely good faith and insistence on the correction are not in tension. The outcome, a missed acknowledgement, still needs fixing regardless of why it happened.

_incorrect.notFinal: Separate the question of intent from the question of outcome. Treating someone with respect does not mean dropping a fix they would likely agree to make.

title: Check 3
instruction: You have raised an unacknowledged contribution in a piece of shared work for {{context}}, and the other person has agreed the acknowledgement should be added. What should you do next to help secure the fairer outcome?

_items.text: Consider the matter closed, since agreement was reached.
Agree a point to check the change has actually been made, since agreement and action are not the same thing.
Ask for the change to be made immediately, in front of you, before the conversation ends.
Raise the same concern again shortly afterwards, in case the first conversation was not taken seriously.

_feedback.correct: An agreement in conversation is not yet a corrected record. Confirming later that the change was actually made is what turns the agreement into the fairer outcome itself.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what still needs to happen after the conversation ends for the correction to actually exist, not just be agreed to.

title: Will it survive the move to a profession?
displayTitle: Will it survive the move to a profession?
body: Each habit below is adequate for most student work. For each one, decide whether it would likely still suffice in a typical profession, or would likely need to tighten.
instruction: Match each habit to the correct category.

_items.text: Citing a source well enough that a marker can identify the text, even if the page number is occasionally approximate.
Keeping a rough mental note of which ideas in a group project came from which member.
Disclosing a conflict of interest whenever one is relevant to a decision.
Correcting a known error in your own work as soon as you notice it.

_feedback.correct: The habits that still suffice are already stated as explicit principles rather than informal practices; professions tend to formalise exactly these. The habits that need to tighten are informal versions of something a profession will typically require to be exact and checkable.

_incorrect.notFinal: Ask whether the habit, as described, is already a formal commitment or an informal approximation that happens to have worked so far.

title: From smallest to largest gap with professional expectations
displayTitle: From smallest to largest gap with professional expectations
body: Four habits of attribution each fall short of a typical profession's expectations by a different margin. Order them from the smallest gap to the largest.
instruction: Drag the habits into order, smallest gap first.

_items.text: Citing the right source but occasionally using an inexact page reference.
Attributing an idea to "the literature" generally, without naming which source it came from.
Assuming verbal credit in conversation is equivalent to a documented acknowledgement.
Treating a contribution as yours to present, because you were the one who wrote it up, regardless of whose idea it originally was.

_feedback.correct: The gap grows as the habit moves from a minor precision issue towards a genuine misattribution of whose work or idea is being presented. A profession's community of practice is typically strict about the latter precisely because it affects who gets credit, and who is accountable, for the underlying work.

_incorrect.notFinal: Weigh how far each habit is from what a formal code of conduct would actually require, not how understandable the habit is in a student context.

title: Worked example: testing a habit against a professional code
displayTitle: Worked example

_items.title: Weaker approach
_items.body: {{learner-a}} has always kept rough, informal notes on where ideas in group work came from, and assumes this habit will carry over fine into professional practice, since it has never caused a problem in coursework. {{learner-a}} does not check it against any actual professional standard before assuming it is adequate.

_items.title: Stronger approach
_items.body: {{learner-b}} has the same informal habit, but deliberately checks it against the code of conduct published by the professional body in their field. {{learner-b}} finds that the code requires a documented, checkable record of contribution for any shared work, not an informal recollection, and concludes the current habit would need to become an explicit written log before it meets that standard.

title: Four reasons professional expectations tighten
displayTitle: Four reasons professional expectations tighten
body: Each reason below explains why a habit adequate for student work often falls short of a profession's standard. Weigh each one before flipping the card to see why it matters.
instruction: Select a card to reveal the reasoning.

_items.title: Higher stakes
_items.back: An error in professional work can affect clients, patients, the public or an organisation's liability, not just a mark on a single piece of work.

_items.title: More expert scrutiny
_items.back: A profession's community of practice is more likely to notice a shortfall than a marker reading dozens of similar essays, because reviewers in the field know exactly what a proper trail looks like.

_items.title: Formal accountability
_items.back: Professional codes of conduct create a documented standard that can be checked and enforced, replacing the informal judgement a tutor might apply.

_items.title: Collective reputation
_items.back: A single lapse can affect how an entire profession is perceived, which is why professional bodies tend to set expectations higher than any one person might set for themselves.

title: Why a community-of-practice lens helps
displayTitle: Why a community-of-practice lens helps
body: Expand each heading to see what applying this lens actually adds.
instruction: Select a heading to expand it.

_items.title: It replaces a personal standard with an external one
_items.body: Checking a habit against a published code removes the risk of simply judging yourself by your own, possibly lenient, sense of what counts as honest.

_items.title: It surfaces gaps before they matter
_items.body: Finding a shortfall in a habit now, as a student, costs far less than finding it after it has already affected professional work.

_items.title: It is specific to the field you are entering
_items.body: Different professions tighten different things; the lens only works once applied to the actual expectations of your field, not a generic idea of "professional conduct".

_items.title: It is something you can repeat
_items.body: Codes of conduct are revised and professions evolve, so the same lens, applied again later, catches a tightening that happens after you have already started practising.

title: Heuristics for critiquing a habit against professional expectations
displayTitle: Heuristics for critiquing a habit against professional expectations
body:
These are checks to weigh against a specific habit of your own, not steps to follow in sequence.

  • Have you checked the actual code of conduct or equivalent standard for your field, rather than guessing what it probably says?
  • Would your current habit produce a documented, checkable record, or only an informal recollection?
  • What would the cost of a shortfall be in a professional setting, compared with in a piece of coursework?
  • Is there a more expert audience in the profession who would notice a gap that a tutor might not?
  • Would the habit need to tighten now, or only once you reach a more senior or more public-facing role?

title: Check 1
instruction: A student keeps an informal mental note of which group member contributed which idea, and has never had this questioned in coursework. What is the strongest critique of this habit when applying a community-of-practice lens?

_items.text: The habit is fine, since it has never caused a problem so far.
The habit relies on informal recollection rather than a documented, checkable record, which many professional codes would require.
The habit is fine as long as the student has a good memory.
The habit only matters if the student plans to work in research.

_feedback.correct: The relevant critique is not about memory or past luck; it is about whether the habit would meet an explicit, checkable standard that a profession's community of practice is likely to require, regardless of how reliable it has felt so far.

_incorrect.notFinal: Separate the question of whether the habit has worked so far from the question of whether it would meet a formal professional standard.

title: Check 2
instruction: Which of these is the strongest example of where a profession's ethical expectations are likely to tighten compared with typical student work?

_items.text: A profession usually expects less detail in citing sources than coursework does.
A profession usually requires a documented, checkable trail of contribution and sourcing, where coursework may accept an informal one.
A profession usually leaves honesty standards entirely to individual judgement, unlike coursework.
A profession usually has no equivalent of a marker checking the work at all.

_feedback.correct: The consistent direction of tightening is towards formal, checkable documentation and away from informal practices that relied on goodwill or an individual's recollection.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about which direction expectations generally move as stakes and scrutiny increase, not whether any particular profession checks work in exactly the same way a marker does.

title: Check 3
instruction: You want to apply a community-of-practice lens to a personal honesty habit relevant to {{context}}. What is the first thing this actually requires you to do?

_items.text: Decide for yourself whether the habit feels honest enough.
Identify the actual professional code or standard for your field and check the habit against its specific requirements.
Assume the habit is fine unless a tutor has ever questioned it.
Wait until you start working in the profession before checking anything.

_feedback.correct: The lens only works once it is applied to the actual, specific expectations of a real professional community, not to a general sense of what seems reasonable or to standards that have never yet been tested.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what makes this a community-of-practice lens specifically, rather than just a personal judgement about honesty.

title: Assigned, or yours to notice?
displayTitle: Assigned, or yours to notice?
body: A new starter encounters each situation below in their first weeks in a role. For each one, decide whether it is something they would normally be explicitly assigned, or something that falls to whoever notices it first.
instruction: Match each situation to the correct category.

_items.text: Completing the specific tasks listed on their induction checklist.
Noticing that a shared record has not been updated in months and nobody seems responsible for it.
Attending the training sessions scheduled for their first month.
Spotting a safeguard that nobody has checked recently and flagging it before it becomes a problem.

_feedback.correct: The distinguishing feature is not how important a task is, but whether it arrives as an explicit instruction or as a gap that simply exists until someone notices it. Unprompted responsibilities are real precisely because no instruction will ever name them directly.

_incorrect.notFinal: Ask whether a new starter would find this task on an induction checklist, or whether it would only become visible to someone who happened to notice it.

title: From least to most initiative required
displayTitle: From least to most initiative required
body: Four situations in a new role call for different amounts of initiative. Order them from the one requiring the least initiative to act on, to the one requiring the most.
instruction: Drag the situations into order, least initiative first.

_items.text: A colleague directly asks you to double-check a figure before it goes out.
You notice a minor inconsistency in a document you were already reviewing for another reason.
You notice a risk in a process that is outside your usual area, with nobody obviously responsible for it.
You notice a risk that would mean questioning a decision made by someone more senior than you.

_feedback.correct: Initiative required tracks how far the situation is from something you were already asked to look at, and how much it might mean challenging an existing decision or crossing into territory that is not clearly yours. The hardest cases are unprompted in every sense: no instruction, no obvious owner, and a power gap to navigate.

_incorrect.notFinal: Weigh how directly each situation connects to something you were already asked to do, and how much standing you would need to raise it.

title: Worked example: a gap nobody assigned
displayTitle: Worked example

_items.title: Weaker approach
_items.body: In their first month in a new role, {{learner-a}} notices that a shared record has not been checked for accuracy in some time, but reasons that since nobody assigned this to them and nobody has complained, it is probably not their responsibility to raise. {{learner-a}} says nothing and moves on to the tasks they were actually given.

_items.title: Stronger approach
_items.body: {{learner-b}} notices the same gap in their own first month. {{learner-b}} recognises that the absence of an assigned owner does not mean the gap is unimportant, and raises it with their supervisor, offering to help correct it. Several months later, when a newer colleague joins the team, {{learner-b}} explains the habit directly: notice what nobody has been explicitly told to check, and raise it rather than assuming someone else already has.

title: Four signs a situation calls for unprompted action
displayTitle: Four signs a situation calls for unprompted action
body: Each sign below can indicate that a situation is an unprompted responsibility rather than something someone else will handle. Weigh each one before flipping the card to see why it matters.
instruction: Select a card to reveal the reasoning.

_items.title: No obvious owner
_items.back: If you cannot name who is actually responsible for the gap, it may be because no one formally is, which makes it everyone's and no one's until someone acts.

_items.title: It has persisted for a while
_items.back: A gap that has existed for some time without being flagged suggests it has already been overlooked by whoever might otherwise have caught it.

_items.title: It would be easy to miss entirely
_items.back: Situations that are easy to miss are exactly the ones that rely on someone noticing without being told to look.

_items.title: The cost of raising it feels disproportionately small
_items.back: If flagging the issue would cost very little, the main reason not to is habit or assumption, not any genuine barrier.

title: Why explaining the habit to someone newer matters
displayTitle: Why explaining the habit to someone newer matters
body: Expand each heading to see why passing a habit on deliberately matters, not just keeping it yourself.
instruction: Select a heading to expand it.

_items.title: It outlasts you
_items.body: A habit that stays in your head only protects whatever you personally notice; explaining it lets someone else notice the next gap after you have moved on.

_items.title: It makes the implicit explicit
_items.body: Unprompted responsibilities are, by definition, never written down; saying them aloud to someone newer is often the only way they get stated at all.

_items.title: It sharpens your own understanding
_items.body: Explaining why you acted, rather than just acting, forces you to articulate the reasoning clearly enough for someone else to apply it in a different situation.

_items.title: It signals that initiative is expected, not just tolerated
_items.body: A new starter who is told explicitly that this kind of noticing is valued is more likely to act on it themselves, rather than assuming it was a one-off.

title: Heuristics for acting on an unprompted responsibility
displayTitle: Heuristics for acting on an unprompted responsibility
body:
These are checks to weigh when you notice something nobody has asked you to deal with, not steps to follow in sequence.

  • Can you actually name who, if anyone, is formally responsible for this?
  • Would the cost of raising it now be smaller than the cost of it staying unaddressed?
  • Are you assuming someone else has already noticed, without any real evidence that they have?
  • If you act on it, could you also explain afterwards why it was worth acting on, to someone newer than yourself?
  • Would waiting to be asked mean waiting for something that was never going to be asked explicitly?

title: Check 1
instruction: A new starter notices a risk in a process that nobody has explicitly asked them to review, and no one else seems to have flagged it either. Which best describes this situation?

_items.text: It is not their responsibility, since it was never formally assigned to them.
It is an unprompted responsibility: one that falls to whoever notices it first, regardless of formal assignment.
It only becomes their responsibility once someone more senior asks them to look into it.
It is someone else's responsibility, since a new starter should not be raising concerns yet.

_feedback.correct: The absence of a formal assignment is exactly what defines this kind of responsibility, not a reason to treat it as someone else's. It falls to whoever notices it, new starter or not.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what actually determines whether something is your responsibility: whether it was formally assigned, or whether you happened to be the one who noticed it.

title: Check 2
instruction: You have identified an unprompted responsibility in a new role. What is the strongest justification for acting on it without waiting to be asked?

_items.text: Acting on it quickly will make a better impression on your manager.
If nobody is formally responsible, waiting to be asked may mean waiting for an instruction that was never going to come.
Every new starter is expected to raise at least one issue in their first month.
Acting on it removes the risk of the issue being noticed by someone else first.

_feedback.correct: The justification is structural, not about impressions or competition: an unprompted responsibility by definition has no one waiting to assign it, so acting is what actually closes the gap.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what would happen to this specific gap if everyone in the role waited to be explicitly asked before acting.

title: Check 3
instruction: You have developed a habit of noticing unprompted responsibilities in a role relevant to {{context}}, and a newer colleague has just joined. What is the most useful way to pass this habit on?

_items.text: Let them notice it in their own time, the way you did.
Explain the habit directly, including why you act on unassigned gaps rather than waiting to be told.
Tell them only once they ask you directly how you handle this kind of situation.
Assume they will pick it up automatically by watching you work.

_feedback.correct: An unprompted responsibility is, by its nature, never written down anywhere a newer colleague would find it. Explaining it directly, including the reasoning, is what makes the habit something the role teaches forward rather than something each person has to discover alone.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about where a habit like this would actually be documented, if anywhere, and what that implies about how a newer colleague would otherwise learn it.
